name: Tea bags on eyes

card.summary: Steeped, cooled tea bags laid on the eyelids to de-puff; the caffeine and tannin rationale is popular, but no trial has tested it.
card.note: Studies exist on the chemistry of tea, not on tea bags as an eye compress.

quick.overview:
Placing used or steeped tea bags over closed eyes is a long-standing home remedy for puffy or dark under-eyes. Proponents attribute the effect to caffeine and tannins, which they say tighten or constrict the skin and vessels around the eye.

No published human study has tested tea bags as an eye compress. Part of the practice may also be the coolness and light pressure of the compress itself.
quick.mechanism: Tea contains caffeine, polyphenols (including tannins and catechins) and other compounds. Chemical analyses show tea infusions contain these substances in varying amounts, and the popular theory is that they act on the skin when applied topically. Whether enough of them cross the eyelid skin to have an effect has not been studied.
quick.risks: The practice is generally described as low risk, though no safety data specific to it were found. Hot bags can scald the thin eyelid skin, and any plant product can cause contact irritation or allergy in some people.

lead: Tea bags on eyes is a home practice in which moistened or steeped tea bags, often chilled, are placed over closed eyelids for several minutes, usually to reduce under-eye puffiness or dark circles. It is a common suggestion in beauty and looksmaxxing discussion of the periorbital area.

Proponents attribute the effect to caffeine, which they describe as a vasoconstrictor, and to tannins, which are described as astringent. Tea does contain caffeine, polyphenols and catechins; chemical analyses of commercially available tea bags report considerable variability in their phenol, catechin and caffeine content.[1][2] Caffeine in tea is reported at roughly 3% of dry weight.[2]

No clinical study has examined tea bags applied to the eyelids. Reference articles on periorbital dark circles discuss anatomical, pigmentary and vascular causes and do not list tea bags among evaluated treatments.[3]
infobox: Steeped, cooled tea bags on closed eyelids

paras: The practice uses ordinary tea bags, most often black or green, which are steeped in hot water, cooled or refrigerated, and held against the closed eyes. Some accounts use herbal teas instead.

Proponents say caffeine narrows blood vessels and tannins tighten skin, reducing swelling and darkness. Laboratory analyses of tea have measured its total phenol, catechin and caffeine contents, which differ widely between products.[1] Those analyses measure the infusion itself and do not address absorption through eyelid skin or any cosmetic effect.[1]
Cold from a chilled bag may contribute to a de-puffing effect independently of the tea; see the entry on cold compresses.

No safety data specific to tea bags on eyes were found. Generic concerns include burns from bags that are too hot, contact irritation or allergy to tea or its additives, and contamination of the eye area.
No studies found. Related research is limited to chemical analysis of tea content and antioxidant capacity, which does not test appearance outcomes.[1]
